ref: G. Bull, Defensio Fidei Nicaenae (1851 tr.), ch. VIII.2 (Hippolytus, threefold sonship)
english: I reply, his meaning manifestly was, that, previous to the Incarnation, the Word had not, so to speak, fulfilled every kind of sonship; or in other words, was not, as yet, the Son of God, in every way in which the Father willed Him to be.
translator: Anonymous translator (not named in the book), in G. Bull, Defence of the Nicene Creed, Oxford: John Henry Parker, 1851
what_it_says: Bull reads Hippolytus's 'perfect Son' remark as a claim that the Logos only fulfilled every kind of sonship at the Incarnation, not that he was imperfect in being.
limits: Bull is a 17th-century defender; this is his explanation, not Hippolytus's words. Arian readers take the 'threefold sonship' reading as subordinationist.

ref: Hippolytus, C. Noet. 15 as quoted and translated in Bull, Defensio (1851 tr.) ch. VIII.2
greek: οὔτε γὰρ ἄσαρκος καὶ καθ᾽ ἑαυτὸν ὁ λόγος τέλειος ἦν καὶ τοι τέλειος λόγος ὢν μονογενὴς, οὐ ἡ σὰρξ καθ᾽ ἑαυτὴν δίχα τοῦ λόγου ὑποστῆναι ἠδύνατο, διὰ τὸ ἐν λόγῳ τὴν ὑπόστασιν ἔχειν
greek_edition: Greek as printed in Bull's footnote (Grabe's notes, Oxford ed.), read from OCR of archive.org defensiofidei01bulluoft; OCR errors likely (e.g. 'καὶ τοι'); NOT collated with Lagarde 1858 or Wendland 1916.
english: For neither was the Word without flesh, and of Himself, perfect Son, whilst yet He was the perfect Word, [being] the Only-begotten: neither could the flesh apart from the Word subsist of itself, forasmuch as it had its ὑπόστασις in the Word, (that is to say, it subsisted in the Word).
translator: Anonymous translator (not named in the book), in G. Bull, Defence of the Nicene Creed, Oxford: John Henry Parker, 1851
what_it_says: Hippolytus says the Word, before the flesh, was perfect Word but not yet perfect Son; the flesh has its subsistence in the Word.
limits: Bull quotes this as cited by the Irenicum author (an Arian-leaning objector) against the Nicene reading; the 'not yet perfect Son' phrase is the core of the subordinationist charge.

ref: Hippolytus, C. Noet. 11 (per NPNF2 vol. 4 note citing 'contr. Noet. 7 and 11' for the Power wording; not confirmed in Lagarde) as quoted in Bull, Defensio (1851 tr.) ch. VIII.2, p. 214
greek: οὐ δύο θεοὺς λέγω, ἀλλ᾽ ὡς φῶς ἐκ φωτὸς, ἢ ὡς ὕδωρ ἐκ πηγῆς, ἢ ὡς ἀκτῖνα ἀπὸ ἡλίου. Δύναμις γὰρ μία ἡ ἐκ τοῦ παντός
greek_edition: Greek as printed in Bull's footnote (quoting Fabricius, Bibl. Graeca XI, p. 18), read from OCR; not collated with Lagarde 1858 or Wendland 1916. Verse-level location (C. Noet. ch.) not fixed by me.
english: When I say that He is another, (that is, the Son from the Father,) I do not say that there are two Gods, but [I say that He is another,] as light from light, and water from a fountain, or a ray from the sun. For the Power from the Whole is one; the Whole, however, is the Father, the Power from whom is the Word.
translator: Anonymous translator (not named in the book), in G. Bull, Defence of the Nicene Creed, Oxford: John Henry Parker, 1851
what_it_says: Hippolytus rejects 'two Gods' for the Son, describing him as Power of the Whole (the Father) like light from light.
limits: The 'Power from the Whole' wording is read by Bull as consistent with Nicene homoousios; Bethune-Baker (item 05) and Newman (item 08) read the same text as the basis of the ditheism charge.

ref: Hippolytus, C. Noet. 12-13 (chapter per the brief, not confirmed in Lagarde) as quoted in Bull, Defensio (1851 tr.) ch. VIII.2, p. 216
greek: Πατὴρ ἐντέλλεται, λόγος ἀποτελεῖ, υἱὸς δὲ δείκνυται δι᾽ οὗ πατὴρ πιστεύεται. Οἰκονομία συμφωνίας συνάγεται εἰς ἕνα Θεόν, εἷς γάρ
greek_edition: Greek as printed in Bull's footnote; read from OCR; not collated with Lagarde 1858 or Wendland 1916. Chapter number as I infer it from Bull's text, not checked in the Greek edition.
english: The Father commands, the Word performs; and the Son is manifested, through whom the Father is believed on. The economy of agreement is gathered up into One God; for God is One; for He who commands [is] Father, He who obeys [is] Son, that which teaches wisdom [is] Holy Ghost. The Father who is above all, the Son through all, and the Holy Ghost in all. Here, as you see, Hippolytus plainly teaches, that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Ghost are one God.
translator: Anonymous translator (not named in the book), in G. Bull, Defence of the Nicene Creed, Oxford: John Henry Parker, 1851
what_it_says: Bull reads Hippolytus's 'economy of agreement' passage as a Trinitarian statement that Father, Son and Spirit are one God.
limits: Bull's reading is a 17th-century apologetic one; the sentences on command and obedience are the ones critics read as subordinationist, and Harnack (item 13) denies an immanent Trinity.

ref: Bethune-Baker, Introduction to the Early History of Christian Doctrine (1903), 'The Theology of Hippolytus', additional note to ch. on Monarchianism, p. 108
english: [Hippolytus's] own theology gave almost equal offence and was charged with ditheism.
translator: n/a (secondary literature; author's own English)
edition: Cambridge: Cambridge University Press (1903 ed.; archive.org introductiontoea0000jfbe)
what_it_says: Bethune-Baker states that Hippolytus was charged with ditheism by his opponents.
limits: A bare statement of the charge; does not say whether the charge was just. Source for the charge is Ref. 9 and Hippolytus's own report of Callistus.

ref: Bethune-Baker (1903), 'The Theology of Hippolytus', p. 108, summary of Dollinger (Hippolytus und Kallistus, 1853)
english: He was the perfect, only-begotten Logos of the Father, but not yet perfect Son: that he first became when he became man.
translator: n/a (secondary literature; author's own English summarising Dollinger)
what_it_says: Bethune-Baker's summary of Dollinger: the Logos becomes Son only at the Incarnation.
limits: A summary of Dollinger's reading, not a verbatim quote from Hippolytus; Bethune-Baker says Dollinger's account is the basis, and he himself lists its problems on p. 109.

ref: Bethune-Baker (1903), 'The Theology of Hippolytus', objections list, p. 109
english: (2) strict subordination: the Son is merely a force to carry out the Father's commands;
translator: n/a (secondary literature; author's own English)
what_it_says: Bethune-Baker lists strict subordination (the Son as the Father's executive force) as one of four doubtful points in Hippolytus's theology.
limits: Lists the objection without deciding it; also lists Logos impersonality and the 'creature' problem as separate points.

ref: Newman, The Arians of the Fourth Century (1833), ch. II sect. III, p. 195
english: Thus Hippolytus says, "When I say that the Son is distinct from the Father, I do not speak of two Gods; but, as it were, light of light, and the stream from the fountain, and a ray from the sun."
translator: John Henry Newman (his own English rendering; no Greek given)
edition: London: J. G. & F. Rivington, 1833 (archive.org theariansofthefo00newmuoft)
what_it_says: Newman cites Hippolytus as an ante-Nicene use of the 'light from light' image that rejects two Gods.
limits: Newman's argument is that the ante-Nicene analogies were defences of Nicene doctrine, which he treats as a historical claim; he also notes they were open to misreading.

ref: Newman, The Arians of the Fourth Century (1833), ch. II sect. IV, p. 215
english: The Fathers, who have laid themselves open to this charge, are Athenagoras, Tatian, Theophilus, Hippolytus, and Novatian, as mentioned in the first chapter.
translator: John Henry Newman (own English; no Greek given)
edition: London: J. G. & F. Rivington, 1833 (archive.org theariansofthefo00newmuoft)
what_it_says: Newman groups Hippolytus with Athenagoras, Tatian, Theophilus and Novatian as writers open to the charge that the Logos was an attribute that became a real person.
limits: Newman's 'charge' is his own reconstruction of the Arian-era objection; the Greek terms he uses are not reproduced here (OCR garbled).

ref: Dollinger, Hippolytus und Kallistus (Eng. 1876), Part II 'The Trinitarian Doctrine of Hippolytus', p. 191
english: his own theology gave offence to the Roman Christians in the opposite direction, and drew on him the charge of Ditheism.
translator: English translation, Edinburgh: T. & T. Clark, 1876; translator not confirmed on the title page I read (preface refers to 'Mr. Plummer')
page: p. 191 (inferred from running header 192 that follows; not checked on a PDF text layer)
what_it_says: Dollinger reports that Hippolytus's own theology, pushed in the opposite direction from Noetus, drew the ditheism charge.
limits: Dollinger's account of the charge; the PDF has no text layer so the page number is OCR-inferred.

ref: Dollinger, Hippolytus und Kallistus (Eng. 1876), Part II, p. 192
english: He was the perfect, only-begotten Logos of the Father, but not yet perfect Son ; He became that first when He became man.
translator: English translation 1876 (translator not confirmed; see above)
what_it_says: Dollinger's exposition: the Logos is perfect Logos but not yet perfect Son until the Incarnation.
limits: Dollinger's exposition of Hippolytus's three stages, not a verbatim Hippolytus quote; Dollinger himself frames it as Hippolytus's view.

ref: Dollinger (Eng. 1876), Part II, p. 193 (threefold stages)
english: [the third moment] is here that He first completes Himself as the true and perfect Son; so that it is also through the Incarnation that the idea of the Divine Fatherhood is first completely realized.
translator: English translation 1876 (translator not confirmed)
what_it_says: Dollinger's three-stage account puts the Son's full sonship at the Incarnation.
limits: Dollinger's reconstruction; the bracketed words are my abbreviation of his sentence, not a change of sense.

ref: Harnack, History of Dogma vol. 2, ch. V (Irenaeus and contemporaries), p. 260-261 (Logos doctrine of Tertullian and Hippolytus)
english: Tertullian and Hippolytus know as little of an immanent Trinity as the Apologists; the Trinity only appears such, because the unity of the substance is very vigorously emphasised; but in truth the Trinitarian process as in the case of the Gnostics, is simply the background of the process that produces the history of the world and of salvation.
translator: Neil Buchanan (tr. of Harnack, History of Dogma, from 3rd German ed.); archive copy is a 1961 printing
edition: Harnack, History of Dogma vol. 2 (archive.org historyofdogma02harnuoft)
what_it_says: Harnack denies that Tertullian or Hippolytus had an immanent Trinity; the Trinity is the background to the world-process.
limits: Harnack's own Logos-theory reading (Gnostic-influenced); a scholarly view that Nicene-era readers reject as reductive.

ref: Harnack, History of Dogma vol. 2, ch. V, p. 260 (Logos in himself)
english: Hippolytus does not share this opinion; to him the Logos in himself is likewise [impassible] (see c. Noetum 15).
translator: Neil Buchanan (tr. of Harnack)
edition: Harnack, History of Dogma vol. 2 (archive.org historyofdogma02harnuoft)
what_it_says: Harnack says Hippolytus, unlike Tertullian, held the Logos in himself to be impassible.
limits: The Greek adjective in the source is garbled in the OCR, so the bracketed word is my reconstruction of Harnack's sense; the Greek is not quoted.

ref: Harnack, History of Dogma vol. 2, ch. V, p. 258 (economy of God)
english: Tertullian and Hippolytus limit the economy of God to Father, Son, and Holy Ghost, while the Gnostics exceed this number.
translator: Neil Buchanan (tr. of Harnack)
edition: Harnack, History of Dogma vol. 2 (archive.org historyofdogma02harnuoft)
what_it_says: Harnack credits Hippolytus with limiting the divine economy to three.
limits: Harnack says the economy is an historical process; the Greek phrase is garbled in the OCR so not quoted.

ref: Athanasius, Select Works and Letters, NPNF2 vol. 4 (1892), editor's note on De Synodis (generation of the Son), page per CCEL page index
english: In other words they seem to teach that He was the Word from eternity, and became the Son at the beginning of all things; some of them expressly considering Him, first as the logos endiathetos, or Reason, in the Father, or (as may be speciously represented) a mere attribute; next, as the logos prophorikos, or Word, terms which are explained, note on de Syn. 26 (5).
translator: Editorial note by Archibald Robertson (editor of NPNF2 vol. 4), English
page: p. 347 (CCEL page index bracket: p. 347 begins before the passage and p. 348 after it; not checked in print)
edition: NPNF2 Series II vol. 4, New York: Christian Literature Co., 1892 (CCEL npnf204)
what_it_says: Robertson reads Hippolytus, with Athenagoras, Tatian, Theophilus and Novatian, as placing the divine generation of the Son just before creation, which he calls the doctrine of Arianism.
limits: Robertson's reading of the 'generation' passages; he also says Bull defends a metaphorical generation (Defensio iii. 5-8).

ref: Hippolytus, C. Noet. 15 as quoted in editor's note, NPNF2 vol. 4 (Athanasius), notes on the Arian 'perfect God' terms
english: Nor was the Word, says Hippolytus, before the flesh and by Himself, perfect Son, though being perfect Word, Only-begotten; nor could the flesh subsist by itself without the Word, because that in the Word it has its consistence: thus then He was manifested One perfect Son of God.
translator: NPNF2 vol. 4 editor's note (Archibald Robertson), English
page: page unknown (CCEL text has no page milestones; index bracket inconclusive)
what_it_says: The editor cites C. Noet. 15 in English: Hippolytus says the Word was perfect Word but not yet perfect Son before the flesh.
limits: Cited as an example of the Arian-friendly 'perfect God' idiom; the editor reads it as close to Arianism.

ref: Robertson, prolegomena to NPNF2 vol. 4 (Athanasius, 1892), section on Roman Monarchianism; page unknown (roman-numbered prolegomena)
english: The theology of Hippolytus was not unlike that of Tertullian, and was hotly charged by Callistus with 'Ditheism.'
translator: Archibald Robertson (editor and prolegomena of NPNF2 vol. 4), English
page: page unknown (roman-numbered prolegomena; CCEL text without page milestones)
what_it_says: Robertson states that Hippolytus was charged with ditheism by Callistus.
limits: A one-line summary; the ditheism charge itself rests on Hippolytus's Ref. 9 and C. Noet.

ref: Eusebius, Church History VI.22.2 (The Works of Hippolytus which have reached us), NPNF2 vol. 1
english: Of his other writings the following have reached us: On the Hexæmeron, On the Works after the Hexæmeron, Against Marcion, On the Song of Songs, On Portions of Ezekiel, On the Passover, Against All the Heresies; and you can find many other works preserved by many.
translator: Arthur Cushman McGiffert (NPNF2 vol. 1, 1890)
page: page unknown (CCEL npnf201 text; no page milestones)
edition: NPNF2 Series II vol. 1, 1890 (newadvent 250106 / CCEL npnf201)
what_it_says: Eusebius lists Hippolytus's surviving works; no title 'Against Noetus' appears, only 'Against All the Heresies'.
limits: Negative: Contra Noetum not named in this list. Eusebius 6.20.2 calls Hippolytus bishop 'of another church' without naming the see.

ref: Jerome, De viris illustribus 61 (Hippolytus), NPNF2 vol. 3 (1892), tr. Ernest Cushing Richardson
english: Hippolytus, bishop of some church (the name of the city I have not been able to learn) wrote A reckoning of the Paschal feast and chronological tables...
translator: Ernest Cushing Richardson (NPNF2 vol. 3)
page: page unknown (NPNF2 vol. 3; newadvent 2708 text; CCEL npnf203 item 61)
edition: NPNF2 Series II vol. 3, 1892 (newadvent 2708 / CCEL npnf203)
what_it_says: Jerome names Hippolytus's works, including 'Against all heresies' and 'Against Marcion', but not 'Against Noetus', and says he did not know the see.
limits: Negative: no 'Against Noetus' title in the list. Jerome also says Origen's commentaries were written in emulation of Hippolytus, a link recorded in the same entry.
